topic: How 99% of the Internet Crosses the Ocean Floor
angle: Most people assume the modern internet lives in space satellites, but nearly all global data flows through hair-thin glass strands wrapped in cables barely thicker than a garden hose, resting unanchored beneath miles of ocean pressure.
why: Massive view counts on infrastructure engineering explainers—such as underwater tunnel construction (18.5M views) and extreme engineering deep-dives (63M+ views)—demonstrate intense global appetite for hidden megaprojects. The contradiction between ethereal 'cloud' computing and dirty, heavy-duty deep-sea physical cables creates an immediate, universal hook for anyone who uses a phone.
keywords: how does the internet cross the ocean
how deep sea cables are laid
facts: Over 95% to 99% of all international internet traffic is carried through undersea submarine cables, while satellites carry only a tiny fraction.
As of 2024, there are more than 550 active and planned undersea fiber optic cables globally, stretching over 1.4 million kilometers.
At the deep ocean bottom, the cable is surprisingly thin—typically between 17 and 21 millimeters in diameter, roughly the thickness of an ordinary garden hose.
In deep open water, cables are unarmored because human hazards like boat anchors are absent; heavy steel armoring is only added near shallow coastal waters.
The data itself travels as pulses of infrared laser light bouncing through glass optical fibers no thicker than a single strand of human hair.
To survive crushing pressures exceeding 800 atmospheres at depths of 8,000 meters, cables contain no hollow air spaces; voids are packed with water-blocking petroleum jelly and solid polymers.
Because light signals weaken after traveling through dozens of kilometers of glass, optical repeaters are spliced into the cable every 50 to 100 kilometers to amplify the signal.
The repeaters require electricity, which is delivered down the length of the cable through an inner copper tube carrying up to 10,000 volts of direct current from shore stations.
Cables are deployed by specialized cable-laying vessels that can hold thousands of kilometers of coiled cable weighing thousands of metric tons in massive internal carousels.
Near shorelines and shallow continental shelves, underwater robotic plows or ROVs dig trenches 1 to 3 meters deep into the seabed to bury and shield the cable from ship anchors and fishing trawlers.
In the deep ocean abyss, the cable is not buried; it is simply unspooled from the ship and left to rest naturally across the seafloor, valleys, and underwater mountain ranges.
In the late 1980s, sharks were recorded biting early subsea cables due to sensitivity to electromagnetic fields, leading engineers to encase sensitive segments in steel protective tape.

Around 100 to 150 undersea cable cuts occur every year worldwide, with roughly 70% caused accidentally by commercial fishing gear and dragging anchors, and the rest caused by underwater landslides or earthquakes.

When a deep-sea cable snaps, specialized repair ships drop grapnel hooks or deploy ROVs to locate the severed ends, haul them to the surface, and splice the microscopic fibers inside cleanrooms on the ship's deck.
Modern transatlantic cables can transmit over 250 terabits of data per second across a single system, enough to stream millions of 4K movies simultaneously.
Subsea fiber cables are engineered for an operational design lifespan of at least 25 years before economic or technological retirement.
